## T1 apparatus — the key decisions (Chunk D)

1. **the memory proves the eternal knower** — the Rāmāyaṇa/Vālmīki example: to say "I was not at
   Rāma's time" is itself a cognition of that time, which implies a knower who persists. Memory
   (smṛti) recollects the prior experience, requiring the stable self.
2. **the Gītā 2.12** — "I was never not" — the eternal knower across the three times.
3. **apūrvaprakāśatva → "the non-unprecedented-manifestation-ness"** — the self is not newly
   manifested; it's the old manifestation (the perpetual light). The body-and-the-rest are the
   "new" manifestations (superimposed).
4. **the pramāṇa/karaṇa (means/instrument)** — the eye-and-the-rest are not self-sufficient
   instruments; they need the agent (kartṛ) and the cognition. The instrument-ness = the
   excellent-service (prakṛṣṭopakāra), not the mere cause.
5. **the sense-organ and the infinite-regress** — if the sense needs another sense to know it
   (the touch), there's an infinite regress; the end (paryanta) is the self-sensation
   (svasaṃvedana) — the self-luminous manifestation.
6. **the pot-example** — "let the pot-reflexion be" — the intention precedes the sense-employment;
   the pot flashes before the sense operates (so the sense isn't the cause).
7. **svasaṃvedana → "self-ascertainment/self-sensation"** — the cognition knows itself; the
   end-instrument of the whole chain.
8. **the three excellences** — (a) in its being, it shines; (b) in its being, it shines alone;
   (c) in its alone-being, it shines — the third is the yogic/manifest direct-perception.
9. **the constructive (vikalpa) = the determination (adhyavasāya)** — the constructive part of
   the manifestation is the excess-over-the-manifest-form, i.e. the exterior-ness. The
   non-constructive (nirvikalpaka) is the manifestation itself.
10. **the vidyā-bhūmi (the knowledge-ground)** — the Śiva/Sadāśiva/Īśvara levels, the
    jñānaśakti-manifestation, the "I-this" with varying clarity.

**The crux:** the cognition and its instrument. Abhinava argues that the self is the eternal
manifestation (not newly-produced), that the sense-organs are only secondary instruments (the
real instrument is the self-luminous cognition), and that the constructive/determination is the
excess-over-the-manifest (the exterior-ness), while the non-constructive is the manifestation
itself. The self-sensation (svasaṃvedana) is the foundation — the cognition knows itself without
an external means. This is the epistemological core of the whole system.


---

# IPVV Vol 1 — Chunk E: the self-as-Lord, the dvairāśya, the cit/acid, the Sāṅkhya — T1

*Source: M00020 lines 2400–3126 (continuous). Base: Torella's ĪPK 1.3 (the "ātmaiva īśvaraḥ"
sūtra's commentary). Covers: the establishedness (siddhatva), the two-fold division
(dvairāśya), the Sāṅkhya pradhāna, the grāhyagrāhaka (grasped-grasper), the
conscious/inert (cit/acid) distinction, the Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi citation, and the refutation of
the "third class." Max-effort T1.*

---

## T1 apparatus — the key decisions (Chunk E)

1. **the cit/acid (conscious/inert) distinction** — the heart: the conscious-form is the
   self-luminous (svayaṃprakāśa); the inert is the not-self-luminous. The two are not of equal
   rank (no tulyakakṣyatā); the co-reference is only metaphorical.
2. **the dvairāśya (two-fold)** — being/non-being, conscious/inert; there's no real third class
   (the Sāṅkhya guṇas are constructions over the experienced).
3. **the grāhyagrāhaka (grasped-grasper)** — the difference-practical-activity of the known and
   the knower is māyā-made; in truth there's one knower.
4. **the Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi citation (v.21)** — "although the object-establishment is restricted
   in the breath-eight-governed jīva, even there it is established in the supreme self; by that
   self alone, how would there be the breath's restraint?" — the direct parallel to our audited
   text.
5. **the Sāṅkhya pradhāna refutation** — the principle (pradhāna) is a construction over the
   experienced pleasure-pain-delusion; its separate-ness is not-established.
6. **the memory/constructive (smṛti/vikalpa)** — the remembered, the constructed, and the
   conjecture all live off the prior experience (the vāsanā); the not-flashing has no
   determination.
7. **the self-luminosity** — "what shines by itself, not by another, is the conscious-form; the
   other is not-in-truth-conscious."
8. **the māyā-position** — in the māyā, the blue-and-the-rest are created (the conscious-unconscious
   appearance); the "I"-part is the full supreme-Śiva; the "this"-part rests in the "I."
9. **the Nareśvaraviveka** ("aṇavaś cidacidrūpāḥ") — the atomic ones, conscious-and-unconscious-form.
10. **the two Gītā citations** — 2.12 (the eternal "I was never not") and 7.10/10.37 (the sixth-case
    determination).

**The crux:** the consciousness/inert distinction and the two-fold. The self-luminous
conscious-form is the real; the inert (and the Sāṅkhya guṇas, the constructions) are not-in-truth
conscious. The māyā is the Lord's own power manifesting the conscious-unconscious appearance.
This is the epistemological-ontological core, engaging the Buddhist (memory/construction) and the
Sāṅkhya (pradhāna) in turn, and citing the Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi (our audited parallel).

# IPVV Vol 1 — Chunk F: the upoddhāta kārikās 1–7, the Buddhist no-self, memory & saṃskāra — T1

*Source: M00020 lines 3126–3700 (continuous). Base: Torella's ĪPK — the upoddhāta (preliminary)
kārikās. Covers: the upoddhāta opening and the division into the two vimarśas; the eleven-verse
synopsis (ślokaikādaśaka); kārikā 1 (svalakṣaṇābhāsaṃ jñānaṃ — the perceptible-cognition),
kārikā 2 (ahaṃpratīti, the I-awareness as body-bound), kārikā 3 (smṛti, memory), kārikās 4–5
(the memory-object, the antargaḍu), kārikā 6 (the smṛtā as a kalpita), kārikā 7 (the varṣātapa
simile). This is the philosophical crux: Abhinava engages the Vijñānavāda (the Buddhist who
denies the self and makes the cognition-series the only reality) on memory and saṃskāra.
Max-effort T1.*

---

## T1 apparatus — the key decisions (Chunk F)

1. **The Buddhist opponent (Vijñānavāda).** Abhinava identifies the real pūrvapakṣa as the
   Saugata — the one who denies the self and makes the cognition-series (jñānasaṃtāna) the only
   reality. The Lokāyatikas are dismissed (they lack a position to refute with); the
   "one-self-with-hidden-lordship" and "many-non-Lord-selves" views are not the primary target.
2. **Kārikā 1 (svalakṣaṇābhāsaṃ jñānam).** The perception (nirvikalpaka, svalakṣaṇa-appearance) is
   one; the vikalpa (constructive cognition) is manifold and articulate (sābhilāpa); the two are
   not reducible. The vikalpa is word-related (śabdasaṃbandhin) — its object is the apoha, the
   general (sāmānya), not the svalakṣaṇa.
3. **The "eka" (one) word** — three readings: (a) rāśi-singularity (the non-constructive class),
   (b) own-form-internal-distinction (no inner class), (c) "some-one-thing." The ṭīkākāra fits the
   middle reading.
4. **Kārikā 2 (ahaṃpratīti as body-bound).** The I-cognition is not the constant self's
   manifestation; it terminates in the body-and-the-rest (śarīrādyavasāyinī). The prayoga: no
   self fitted with permanence, because of non-perception of what is perceptible-by-nature.
5. **The sābhilāpa (articulate) viśeṣaṇa** — the I-cognition is articulate; its articulation is
   non-deviating (abhilāpāvyabhicāra). The "ahaṃ" is not a bare inner grasp but an articulate
   cognition, which is why the avasāyinī-ending (tendency-to-end) shows its constructedness.
6. **Kārikā 3 (smṛti).** Memory proves the constant self: in the destruction of experience, the
   memory that follows the experience (tadanurodhinī) could not be, unless the experiencer is a
   stable self. The siddhāntin's own reply: the experience is destroyed outward (bahirmukha) but
   undestroyed inward (antarmukha) — self-perception (svasaṃvedana) survives.
7. **The three gatis (courses) for the sarvajña** — (a) constant awareness comprehending past-
   present-future; (b) the non-constant cognition-series with the samanantarapratyaya carrying
   the object's direct-manifestation; (c) the pure appearance of the wanted object. All three
   show memory cannot have an independent object.
8. **Kārikās 4–5 (the antargaḍu).** The siddhāntin: memory arises from the prior-experience
   impression (saṃskāra), so it lives on the experience, not on the constant self. The objector
   answers: then the "inside-stake" self (antargaḍu) has no purpose. The refutation: the outward-
   face part (the imitation, anukaraṇa) alone survives as the impression — the inward self-
   luminous awareness is not needed.
9. **The bhūrja-leaf simile** — the non-constant continuum still shows imitation (anukaraṇatā):
   the rolled-unrolled leaf, the arrow's velocity (vega), the river. The saṃskāra is essentially
   anukaraṇa (imitation), not a fixed dharma in a constant substrate. The kūṭastha-eternal is
   rejected; only saṃtāna-nityatā holds.
10. **Kārikā 6 (smartā as kalpita).** If memory is established from the impression alone, the
    rememberer (smartā) is constructed like the seer (draṣṭā) — a kalpita, not a real self. The
    I-cognition (ahaṃpratīti) does not reveal the self, only the body/continuum.
11. **The saṃskāra-dharmin debate.** The impression cannot inhere in the continuum (which is not a
    real dharmin beyond the cognitions); experience and impression are non-different by the
    support-identity (āśrayābheda). The one support is the constant self — but that very
    constancy makes it unusable in generating the memory (no viśeṣa).
12. **Kārikā 7 (the varṣātapa simile).** The sky-leather simile: as rain and heat have no fruit on
    the sky (the unchanging), so the constant self cannot produce memory. The leather-like
    (changing) is non-eternal; the sky-like (constant) is like the non-existent. The general
    principle (niyamavat): a construction is only justified if it is capable of its end.
13. **The crux.** The whole passage turns on whether memory (smṛti) requires a constant self. The
    Buddhist says no — the saṃskāra/anukaraṇa in the cognition-series suffices; the eternal self
    is a vain hypothesis (vyartha kalpanā). Abhinava (as the siddhāntin) is here giving the
    pūrvapakṣa its strongest form before refuting it later in the vimarśa.

**Cross-references:** Yogasūtra 1.9/1.11 (vikalpa, smṛti definitions) and 3.18 (saṃskāra-
sākṣātkaraṇa); Vākyapadīya 2.130 (the abhijalpa); ĪPK 1.18 (dṛk svabhāsaiva). The Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi
argument (consciousness as self-luminous, svayaṃprakāśa) is the doctrinal parallel to the
siddhāntin's antarmukha svasaṃvedana.

# IPVV Vol 1 — Chunk G: the jñāna/cit refutation, kārikās 7–8 (the consciousness-form), the Sāṅkhya buddhi — T1

*Source: M00020 lines 3700–4300 (continuous). Base: Torella's ĪPK — the upoddhāta continuation.
Covers: the conclusion of kārikā 6 (the yasminsati verse), the refutation of the jñāna-reason
(kārikā 7: jñānaṃ ca citsvarūpaṃ cettadanityaṃ kimātmavat), the cit/acid (conscious/inert)
distinction, the Sāṅkhya's buddhi-as-vṛtti (kārikā 8: caitanyam ajaḍā), the ābhāsa/vyavasthā
(appearance/establishment), the bhoga (enjoyment), and the puruṣa/buddhi relation. The heart of
the passage: the jñāna-cognition cannot be the self's action (dharma) without inheriting the
self's own eternity/pervasion/oneness, and the inert (jaḍa) cannot manifest the object.
Max-effort T1.*

---

## T1 apparatus — the key decisions (Chunk G)

1. **Kārikā 6's conclusion.** The yasminsati-verse establishes the pervasion of the reason
   (vyāpaka): a construction is justified only as the cause of its effect (taddhetutvena), else
   there is infinite regress of reasons (hetūnām anavasthitiḥ). The constant self is such a
   groundless construction for the Buddhist.
2. **Kārikā 7 (jñānaṃ ca citsvarūpaṃ cettadanityaṃ kimātmavat).** The core refutation of the
   jñāna-reason: if the cognition (jñāna) is of the consciousness-form (citsvarūpa) like the
   self, then it is eternal like the self (and the dharmi-hetu relation collapses — a dharma
   cannot differ from its dharmin in both being and non-being); if it is inert (jaḍa), it cannot
   manifest the object (nārthaprakāśatā).
3. **The svaprakāśa (self-luminous).** The consciousness-form's characteristic is self-luminous-
   ness; this is opposed (viruddha) to being-known (vedyarūpatva), which is the other-manifested
   (paraprakāśyatā). Freedom and dependence (svātantrya/pāratantrya) are opposed. So the
   cognition cannot be both conscious and known — hence non-eternal.
4. **The dṛṣṭānta (example) logic.** The "ātmavat" example is used by sādharmya (similarity), not
   vaidharmya (difference). The gloss on the negation: "kim... na anityam" — "why not non-eternal,"
   i.e. "not non-eternal," a prasajyapratiṣedha.
5. **The Jaiminīya and Sāṅkhya positions.** The Jaiminīyas take the person as cognition-form
   (saṃvidrūpa) with distinct states; the Sāṅkhyas as pure self-perception (svasaṃvedana), non-
   transforming (apariṇāmin). Both fall under the same prasaṅga.
6. **The deśa-kāla (place-time) restriction (saṃkoca).** The place-time are the known (vedya) that
   would contract (saṃkocaka) the cognition. But the awareness (bodha) is of a different rank
   (bhinnakakṣya) from place-time: it shines as "I" (aham) with freedom, while place-time shine
   as "this" (idam) dependent on the other. A different-rank thing cannot contract one of a
   higher rank (as the sky cannot be contracted by the underworld). Cited: ĪPK 1.52
   (kevalaṃ bhinnasaṃvedyadeśakālānurodhataḥ).
7. **The Sāṅkhya buddhi.** The buddhi-tattva is the "instrument aggregate" (karaṇaskandha), the
   first transformation (mahān) of the pradhāna; inert (jaḍa) by itself but appearing-cognitive
   (cetanavat) through the person's reflection (puruṣapratibimba). This is figurative awareness
   (upacaritabodha).
8. **Kārikā 8 (caitanyam ajaḍā).** If the cognition were neither wholly conscious nor wholly
   inert, the Sāṅkhya proposes the buddhi that takes on the object's form (rūpa) and the self's
   consciousness (caitanya) by reflection. Abhinava's refutation: the inert cannot arrange the
   objects (vyavasthā), and the conscious cannot both be and not-be non-inert — the two (cid/acid)
   are utterly opposed in one substance.
9. **The viśrānti (rest).** The object-cognitions rest (viśrānti) in the experience-determination-
   form consciousness; the unconscious object cannot establish (vyavasthāpayet) the distinct
   states (vyavasthā) of blue/yellow. This is the "establishedness" that needs a non-inert ground.
10. **The vṛtti (operation) as transformation.** The Sāṅkhya's vṛtti is a transformation-particular
    (pariṇāmaviśeṣa): the buddhi's operation is the cognition. The three types (kārya, dharma,
    vṛtti pariṇāma) are distinguished; the cognition is the vṛtti-transformation.
11. **The sāmānādhikaraṇya (co-reference).** "Buddhi = jñāna" is not a genuine identity but the
    aggregate-well-knownness (samudāyaprasiddhi) over the parts — the weak action-meaning is
    absorbed. So the co-reference removes the bodhatā-doubt.
12. **The phala (result).** The cognition-action's result is the sattva-part (sattvāṃśa), the
    light/manifesting guṇa. The sattva is pure (śuddha), the rajas dispels the tamas-cloud; only
    then does it manifest the blue-and-the-rest and the pleasure-and-the-rest. The fruit is the
    consciousness-shadow (saṃvicchāyā) — the undifferentiated personal citta-vṛtti-awareness.
13. **The bhoktṛ-bhogya (enjoyer-enjoyed).** The enjoyment (bhoga) is the mixing (melana) of the
    self- and object-reflections in the buddhi — not a property of the external object
    (prakaṭatā). The self as direct seer (sākṣāt draṣṭā) does not produce the manifest-ness; the
    ahaṃkāra mediates the superimposition (upakārakatva) that makes the self appear as agent.

**The crux.** The whole passage is the pūrvapakṣa's assault on the jñāna-reason for lordship: the
self's knowledge cannot be a real dharma (else eternal/pervading/one like the self) nor an inert
thing (else no manifestation). The Sāṅkhya's buddhi is the most sophisticated answer (reflection-
based cognition), and it is refuted in detail — the inert cannot arrange, the conscious cannot
contract, the enjoyment needs the non-inert consciousness as its ground. The jñānādhikāra's core
(svaprakāśa consciousness, viśrānti, svātantrya) is here exercised against the Sāṅkhya.

**Cross-references:** ĪPK 1.52 (the krama/pratibhāsa verse); Sāṅkhyakārikā 13 (sattvaṃ laghu
prakāśakam), 18 (pratiniyama), 29 (svālakṣaṇyaṃ vṛttir trayasya); Yogasūtra 1.6 (vṛttayaḥ
pañcatayyaḥ), 1.2 bhāṣya (citiśaktirapariṇāminī); Yogadarśana; Nareśvaraviveka (na hi yathā
gotvaṃ). The Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi parallel: the self as self-luminous non-inert knower, over against
the inert and the reflection-based Sāṅkhya buddhi.

# IPVV Vol 1 — Chunk H: the reflection (pratibimba) argument, the mirror & echo — T1

*Source: M00020 lines 4300–5077 (continuous). Base: Torella's ĪPK — the continuation of the
caitanyam ajaḍā discussion. Covers: the bhoga as the mixing of reflections in the buddhi; the
ahaṃkāra's superimposition; the saṃyoga/samavāya relation; the reflection-argument in full (the
mirror-reflection, the echo pratiśrutkā, the taste-reflection, the smell-field); the Sāṅkhya
buddhi's reflection of the puruṣa refuted; the vākyapadīya citations; the jñāna and jñātatā
(cognizedness) — whether the object's manifestness (prakaṭatā) is a real dharma of the object or
the cognition itself; the Nyāyasūtra adhikaraṇasiddhānta; the conclusion that only the cognition
(jñāna) is the cognizedness, the prakāśa. Max-effort T1.*

---

## T1 apparatus — the key decisions (Chunk H)

1. **The bhoga (enjoyment) as reflection-mixing.** The enjoyment is the one-ness (aikya) operated in
   the buddhi-determination (adhyavasāya) between the person's reflection and the object's reflection
   — not a real property of the external object. The Yogasūtra 3.35 (sattvapuruṣayor pratyayāviśeṣo
   bhogaḥ) is the anchor.
2. **The ahaṃkāra's superimposition.** The ahaṃkāra makes the not-enjoying, faultless self appear as
   the agent-enjoyer (upakārakatva) — a figurative treatment (upacāra) that creates a new cognition-
   word-particular in the figurative-treater alone.
3. **The saṃyoga/samavāya (conjunction/inherence).** Whether the bhoga is by saṃyoga or samavāya is
   indifferent (ko virodhaḥ?) — any relation suffices; the practical activity (vyavahāra) of enjoyment
   is contact-made (saṃsargakṛta) in all views (paropādhau sarvā dhīr vyāvahārikī).
4. **The Sāṅkhya's bhoktṛ refuted.** The pradhāna transforms (pariṇamate); the jaḍa (inert) cannot be
   the enjoyer; only the cidrūpa (conscious-form) is fit for enjoyment, and its multiplicity follows
   from pratiniyama (Sāṅkhyakārikā 18). The bhoga's anāditva would block liberation — resolved by
   viveka (discrimination).
5. **The svacchatva (clearness) rule.** A clear thing reflects only a more-clear thing (as the white
   cloth reflects in the crystal, not vice versa). The buddhi is less clear than the person; the
   person's manifestation (puruṣaprakāśa) is all-sides-clear (sarvataḥ svaccha) and expects nothing
   (ananyāpekṣa). The buddhi cannot reflect the person — the cause-opposed perception
   (kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi).
6. **The reflection-rule (anvaya-vyatireka).** A mirror reflects only the form-arrangement (rūpasaṃsthāna),
   not heaviness/touch. The pure dense form is needed; taint blocks it. The Tantrāloka 3.6 (the concealed
   lover touching the mirror) is cited.
7. **The Naiyāyika view.** Reflections are errors (bhrānti) — the repelled eye-rays grasp the own face.
   Abhinava's refutation: the own-face-as-other would make us indifferent to ornaments; the child's
   single-flavored cognition ("this") shows it; the reflection (pratibimba) is a real third class
   (tṛtīyarāśiḥ), not mere error. The vastutva (being) of the reflected is denied only by the 
   vyāpakānupalabdhi of the "this-being-that-class" (sajātīya).
8. **The pratiśrutkā (echo).** The echo is a real reflection of the sound, not a distinct primary sound:
   its faintness at a distance (the hearers' inversion), the Tantrāloka 3.29 and 3.34 (the sound-
   reflection verses), and the śruti-timing. The Naiyāyika's "sound travels" (śabdajaśabda) is rejected.
9. **The rasa (taste)-reflection.** The pungent taste of the pomegranate appears in the other's teeth-
   water (dantodaka) as a reflection (rasāveśa), proved by the avadhāna-awakening; the pomegranate-
   juice tasted-in-own-mouth objection is refuted. The reflected taste in the other's mouth is not
   experienced — because the field is interior (antardehavṛtti).
10. **The avabhāsana (manifestation) as the essence.** The reflection is essentially manifestation
    (avabhāsanasāra) — not place, form, measure, etc. (Tantrāloka 3.23, the darpaṇavidhi). It depends
    on the inner organ's operation (antaḥkaraṇavyāpāra) engaging the sense-organ.
11. **The Sautrāntika/Devala.** Even the Sautrāntika's cognition-reflection needs the primary non-inert
    conscious power (mukhyā ajaḍā citiśakti) to arrange the objects; the Devala verse (puṃsi kartṛtvam
    āropya) is cited. The reflection cannot make the inert do the arranging.
12. **The satkāryavāda (Sāṅkhyakārikā 9, asadakaraṇāt).** The self cannot be the material cause
    (upādāna) of the buddhi: the effect's being is in the cause-complex (sāmagrī), not in one material
    cause. The kaivalya (isolation) would force the person to gain/lose the effect-remainder (kāryaśeṣa),
    an impossible opposition of dharmas — hence the person is not the transforming material cause.
13. **The anubhavabala (experience-force).** Only one conscious self-luminous tattva (the experience)
    is established by experience-force; the "self-reflection" and "consciousness-shadow" of the buddhi
    are not separately given. The 'ahaṃ' is the self-luminous cognition itself, not a dharma of a
    transcendent person. The bandhamokṣa (bondage-liberation) is operated in the person by a superimposed
    relation — its karmapravacanīya force is scrutinized.
14. **The jñāna-jñātatā (the cognition is the cognizedness).** The object's manifest-ness (prakaṭatā) is
    not a real dharma of the object (else infinite regress: the manifest object would need another
    manifesting); it is the cognition itself (jñānameva jñātatā). The cognition is pratyakṣa by
    self-perception (svasaṃvedana), established by the adhikaraṇasiddhānta (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.30). The
    jñātatā is not universal (not toward all knowers), so it is the cognition, not the object-form.
15. **The hetu-grammar.** The long discussion of yasmāt/tataḥ in the anuvāda (restating) — whether the
    reason is the stated fact or its cognition. The ancient practice (cirantana) used the fifth case in
    restating (yato hi pūrvānubhavasaṃskārāt, ĪPK 2.5); the moderns live on prasiddhi only. The
    distinguished-reason (viśiṣṭahetuka) is the valid one.
16. **The svaprakāśa-jñāna as the self.** If the self-luminous cognition is established, is it the self?
    Abhinava: its place/time differences (jñeyopādhi — "here the pot", "now the pot") are cognized-made
    and body-limited (for the pleasure-cognition), so it is not the eternal-pervading-one self — but the
    cognitions as place-time-distinct flow in a continuum (saṃtati), which is the world-course. This
    sets up kārikā 9 (kriyā): the action too cannot be a real dharma of the object (the body) nor one
    single action in a sequential (kramika) one.

**The crux.** Chunk H is the deepest engagement yet with the reflection-metaphysic: whether the 
cognition can be a reflection (of the object) in a substrate (the buddhi) — the Sāṅkhya's view — or
must be the self-luminous consciousness itself (the siddhānta). The answer: reflections are real
(appearance-based), but the cognition is not such a reflection in an inert buddhi; the clear
(svaprakāśa) consciousness alone can arrange the objects (vyavasthā) and enjoy (bhoga). The
manifestation (avabhāsana) is the essence of both reflection and cognition; and the cognition is
ultimately self-luminous — the manifestness of the object is the cognition itself (jñānameva
jñātatā).

**Cross-references:** Yogasūtra 3.35 (pratyayāviśeṣo bhogaḥ); Sāṅkhyakārikā 3 (na prakṛtir na
vikṛtiḥ puruṣaḥ), 9 (asadakaraṇāt), 18 (pratiniyamāt), 31 (puruṣārtha eva hetuḥ); Nyāyasūtra 1.1.30
(adhikaraṇasiddhānta); Vākyapadīya 2.37 (upādāyāpi ye heyāḥ); Tantrāloka 3.6, 3.23, 3.29, 3.34; ĪPK
2.5 (yato hi pūrvānubhavasaṃskārāt). The Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi parallel: the self as the self-luminous
non-inert knower whose manifestness of the object is its own cognition.

# IPVV Vol 1 — Chunk I: the kriyā (action) and the kāryakāraṇabhāva (cause-effect) — T1

*Source: M00020 lines 5077–5585 (continuous). Base: Torella's ĪPK — kārikā 9 (kriyāpy arthasya
kāyādes) on the action as not a separate real thing, and kārikā 10 (tatra tatra sthite) on the
cause-effect relation. Covers: the definition of kriyā as the sequential-parts (pūrvāparībhūta-
bhāga) operation, the grammarian Bhartṛhari citations (the āśritakrama verses), the ātman's
jñāna/icchā/kriyā, the relation (saṃbandha) refuted as a real third thing, and the
kāryakāraṇabhāva as the prior/posterior-being (pūrvatva/paratva) of the two relata. Max-effort T1.*

---

## T1 apparatus — the key decisions (Chunk I)

1. **Kārikā 9 (kriyāpy arthasya kāyādes).** The action is not a real separate thing; the 
   body-and-the-rest (kāyādi) only has "the birth of the new-new in place-place" 
   (tattaddeśādijātatā). The action is not other (nānyā) — because of non-perception (adṛṣṭeḥ);
   nor is it one and sequential (na sāpyekā kramikā) — because the sequential cannot be one.
2. **The kriyā-characteristic.** The action (kriyā) is the operation (vyāpāra) related to the
   operator (kāraka), its parts (bhāgāḥ) being prior-later-opposed (pūrvāparībhūtāḥ) and sequence-
   operating (kramavṛttayaḥ). The Bhartṛhari citations (āśritakramarūpatvāt tatkriyeti) anchor this.
3. **The īśvara's action.** For the Lord-self-speakers, the self does have the action: "desires,
   knows, strives" (icchati jānāti yatate) — cited from ĪPK 1.3, 1.6, 1.24 (tadecchā tāvatī,
   evaṃ na jātu cittasya, ghaṭādigrahakāle tu ghaṭaṃ jānāti sā kriyā).
4. **The bhāgas (parts).** The parts of the "knows"-action (intention, lamp, etc.) are not themselves
   prior or later (apūrvāpare) but only prior-later-opposed by mutual expectation. The objection
   "let them just be the action by their own form" is rejected — that would destroy the 
   āśritakramatva (the sequential-form-ness) that is sought.
5. **The avayavī/aggregate refuted.** The action cannot be a whole (avayavī) — the sequential cannot
   be begun by non-sequential parts; nor an aggregate (samudāya) — because of non-simultaneity 
   (ekakālatvābhāvāt), unlike the army (senā) whose members are simultaneous. Nor even the parts
   alone — that would yield only difference (bheda), but the prior-later-being requires a 
   non-difference-touch (abhedasparśa).
6. **The one-action by cognition.** The oneness of the action (ekā kriyā) is cognition-determined
   (buddhyā vikalparūpayā adhyavaseyam) — the parts' prior-later-being is a construction over them.
   This is not rootless: it follows from the one-operator (ekakāraka) — the agent-object oneness
   (kartṛkarmaikya) and the one-fruit (ekaphaloddeśa).
7. **The ākhyāta's number.** The number (saṃkhyā) in "cooks" is the agent-object-gone (kartṛkarmagata),
   not the action's own; the 'eka' word means only difference-absence (bhedābhāvamātra). The
   action is ayutā (united) with the substance — by inherence or identity, not separate.
8. **The pratyabhijñā of the substance.** The one operator-substance is established by recognition
   (aikyapratyabhijñānāt — "sa eva ayaṃ caitra"). The action is inferred as the kārakātirikta
   kramika vastu: if the substance alone produced the fruit it would be before; if the other, then
   not expected; so there is a sequential distinct thing — the action. But this inference (from
   pratyabhijñāta substance + fruit) is itself refuted by the opposer (bādhaka): the fruit is not
   established from the recognized one substance.
9. **The bhāvanā (Mīmāṃsaka).** The action can also be the bhāvanā (the generated-operation, 
   jananātmā vyāpāraḥ) of the person in the to-be-effected heaven — the kriyāpy arthasya reading 
   via arthāpatti. The ṭīkākāra uses the Buddhist view to refute the Kaṇāda/Sāṅkhya/Mīmāṃsaka 
   cognition-views after the relation-refutation sūtra.
10. **The āśraya (support) refuted.** The sequential action cannot inhere in one support: the prior
    and later parts differ both in own-form and time, which forces the one support to have
    opposite dharmas (viruddhadharmādhyāsa) in four ways (caturdhā). The time-difference is
    universal (sārvatrika) and ends in own-form-difference; the place-difference is not universal.
11. **The samūha (aggregate) and āśritakrama.** The "sequence-possessing-like non-sequential ones"
    (āhitottaraśaktitvāt... kramavanta ivākramāḥ) is refuted — the 'iva' shows the unreality of the
    sequence; the later instants receive no power from the prior. The action is the mere new-being
    (apūrvajanmamātra) of the cognition-form in each time.
12. **The pariṇāma (transformation).** The action gathers under "transformation" (pariṇāma): both
    the place-difference-ones (growth/decline) and the time-sequence-ones (standing, sitting, 
    knowing, remembering, desiring). "Goes" = place-difference; "stands the day" = time-difference;
    "it blues/whitens" = own-form-difference. So the place-time-own-form-other-ness IS the action.
13. **Kārikā 10 (tatra tatra sthite).** There-there standing, "this becomes that" alone is seen;
    there is no other relation (nānyo'sti saṃbandhaḥ) besides the effect-cause-relation
    (kāryakāraṇabhāva). The relation is not a third thing beyond the two relata.
14. **The kāryakāraṇabhāva.** The cause-effect relation is just the prior-ness/later-ness
    (pūrvatva/paratva) of the two own-forms: the one whose being precedes (prayojakasattākaḥ) is
    prior (the cause), the one whose being follows (prayojyasattākaḥ) is later (the effect). The
    two are seen simultaneously in one perception (sakṛtpravṛttapratyakṣa) — "smoke-being when 
    fire, not when no fire" — the anvaya-vyatireka. Cited the two śloka on the kāryabuddhi.
15. **The relation as case-meaning.** Both the seventh case (tatra) and the genitive (rājñaḥ) and
    the operator-cases (kārakavibhakti) mean only the effect-cause-relation — there is no other
    relation-thing. The relation is not one-time (naikakālikam): in the fire's being there is no
    smoke, in the smoke's time the fire-instant is gone; so the "one relation" is a construction
    (vikalpa), not a real thing. Cited: ityamiśrāḥ svayaṃ bhāvāstānyojayati kalpanā.
16. **The sattāniṣedha.** The refutation of the relation's being (sattā) is by the opposer-pramāṇa
    (bādhaka) — dviṣṭhasya (kārikā 11) up to pāratantryādyayogāt — combined with kārikā 10's
    "nānyo'sti." So "there is no other relation" is established by the two sūtra-parts together; 
    the future sūtra's pañcamī (tena) will then state the reason.

**The crux.** Chunk I refutes the action (kriyā) and the relation (saṃbandha) as real separate
things, to destroy the jñānakriyāyogāt-reason for the self's lordship. The action is only the
place/time/own-form-difference (the new-being) in the substance, gathered by cognition into a
"one" sequential thing; the relation is only the effect-cause prior/later-ness of the two relata.
Both are constructions (kalpanā), not pāramārthika — exactly parallel to the jñāna's rejection in
Chunk H. This completes the destruction of the second part (kriyā) of the jñāna-kriyā-yoga reason,
setting up kārikā 11 (tena kartāpi kalpitaḥ) in Chunk J.

**Cross-references:** ĪPK 1.3 (tadecchā), 1.6 (evaṃ na jātu), 1.24 (ghaṭādigrahakāle); Bhartṛhari 
Vākyapadīya (the āśritakrama and kriyā verses, the bhāgāḥ pacateḥ); Sāṅkhyakārikā; Mīmāṃsā (bhāvanā); 
Nyāya (kriyā as karmapadārtha); the pratyabhijñā (sa eva ayaṃ caitra). The Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi parallel:
the self's action is its cognition (jñānam eva kriyā), not a separate sequential operation.

# IPVV Vol 1 — Chunk J: kārikā 11 (tena kartāpi kalpitaḥ), the relation refuted, the pūrvapakṣa's close — T1

*Source: M00020 lines 5585–5750 (continuous). Base: Torella's ĪPK — kārikā 11 (dviṣṭhasyānekarūpatvāt,
siddhasyānyānapekṣaṇāt, pāratantryādyayogācca, tena kartāpi kalpitaḥ). Covers: the consolidation of the
four-fold absence (abhāvacatuṣṭaya), the relation (saṃbandha) refuted by the bādhaka (opposer), the
apekṣā (expectation) as the supposed relation and its rejection, the pāratantrya (dependence), the
rūpaśleṣa (form-adhesion), the Bhartṛhari verses on the relation, and the conclusion that the agent
(kartā) is constructed (kalpita) — the close of the pūrvapakṣavimarśa (the second vimarśa). Max-effort T1.*

---

## The genitive, the pāratantrya, the rūpaśleṣa, the Bhartṛhari verses

**Objection (nanu):** "[And]-of-the-existing-then (satostarhi), [and]-the-expectation (apekṣā), [and]-will-be (bhaviṣyati), [and]-like-'of-the-king-the-man (rājñaḥ puruṣa itivat)'" — [and]-this (etat), [and]-he-removes (nirasyati): "and-not (naca iti)". ## T1 apparatus — the key decisions (Chunk J)

1. **The four-fold absence (abhāvacatuṣṭaya).** The kārikā 11's reason (tena) consolidates four
   absences: (i) no other relation (nānyo'sti saṃbandhaḥ), (ii) no other action (nānyad asti — the
   kriyā is not a real separate thing), (iii) the relation's being-determination-absence, and
   (iv) its non-being-determination. These together make the agent constructed (kartāpi kalpitaḥ).
   The ṭīkā states this via the fifth case (abhāvāt).
2. **The bādhaka (opposer) for the relation.** The relation's universal absence is established not
   by the bare non-perception of the seen (which only yields "not here-now") but by the opposition
   (virodha) internal to the other's own acknowledged form — the two-form opposition. The citation
   (iṣṭaṃ viruddhakārye'pi deśakālādyapekṣaṇam) anchors the place-time-restricted non-being.
3. **The sāmānyalakṣaṇa refutation.** What stands simultaneously in two, with own-form-completion,
   is not one — like the two pots in two houses. Oneness = non-distinct-form (abhinnarūpatva); the
   two-established-ness (dviṣṭhatva) is pervaded by the distinct-form, so the one-relation is
   negated by the opposed-pervaded-perception (tadviruddhavyāptopalabdhi).
4. **The apekṣā (expectation) as relation.** The genitive ("of the king") prompts an expectation —
   the relation is said to be this expectation. But the expectation is only the helper-object
   (upakārakaviṣaya): the inert (jaḍa) cannot expect (apekṣā pāratantryaṃ ca na saṃbandho jaḍātmanoḥ);
   the non-transcendent helper would just be the cause (kāraṇa); the existing (sat) cannot expect
   (saṃś ca sarvanirāśaṃso bhāvaḥ katham apekṣate). The practical-activity (vyavahāra) is the
   construction (vikalpa) of the practical-activity-doer, not the relation-thing.
5. **The genitive and the effect-cause.** "Of the king, in the man existing" — the expectation is
   one-gone (the genitive) and the other-gone (the locative), not a mutual expectation. The
   mutual-expectation (parasparāpekṣā) and dependence (pāratantrya) are also refuted: the mutual-
   facing-ness (unmukhatā) is a mere word, not a shared relation. Even here the effect-cause-relation
   (kāryakāraṇabhāva) is what rests.
6. **The rūpaśleṣa (form-adhesion).** The "mutual form-obtainment" (paraspararūpā prāpti, like the
   fingers) fails: two forms cannot adhere; if adhesion is oneness, it is no relation
   (dvitve sati kathaṃ bhavet).
7. **The Bhartṛhari relation-verses.** The relation has no word expressive of it by its own dharma
   (nābhidhānaṃ svadharmeṇa saṃbandhasyāsti vācakam); it is followed only through its helper
   (upakārāt sa yatrāsti dharmastatrānugamyate); it is the power of powers, the quality of
   qualities. Abhinava notes this is a stotra (praise), not a nyāya-statement — hence not refuted.
8. **The kāryakāraṇabhāva not applicable here.** The self is not the effect; the cognition does not
   make the self its cause (via the yasminsati maxim — the infinite-regress); the action is nothing;
   so no relation here at all. This is the tatsamāśraya point: the verb-root says the action, the
   suffix says the agent, but no relation joins them.
9. **The jñātṛtā (knower-ness).** The experience-construction-memory-cognition-series alone exists,
   not a knower. The example: in the knower-ness there is the cognition but no other/relation; in
   the other-agent-ness there is no action, no other, no relation — so the agent is constructed
   (kalpitaḥ). The cognition-action too is refuted (as a kriyā, whether dhātvartha for the grammarian
   or pratyayavācya for the bhāvanā-Mīmāṃsaka). This is the firmest part of the debate.
10. **The close of the pūrvapakṣavimarśa.** The vṛttikṛt's phala (fruit) of the whole nanu-
    svalakṣaṇābhāsaṃ...tena kartāpi kalpitaḥ passage: "How can the self be the all-Lord?"
    (katham ātmā sarveśvaraḥ). The dharmin-unestablished (jñānasyaiva bodhātmanaḥ) and the reason-
    unestablished (kriyākāraka iti tāvanmātralakṣaṇam) are shown; the svabhāva-hetu for the lordship-
    practical-activity-establishment is absent. The Buddhist establishes the cognition-continuum-
    alone (jñānasaṃtatimātram) as the self. The pūrvapakṣavimarśa (the second vimarśa) closes here.

**The crux.** Chunk J completes the Buddhist's pūrvapakṣa: having refuted the self (dharmin), the
cognition (jñāna), the action (kriyā), and the relation (saṃbandha), the reason "from the 
knowledge-action-joining, lordship" (jñānakriyāyogād aiśvaryam) is entirely destroyed — neither the
knower-ness nor the agent-ness is established. The agent (kartā) is constructed (kalpitaḥ) like the
seer (draṣṭā) was in kārikā 6. Only the cognition-continuum (jñānasaṃtati) remains — the Buddhist
view. This is the complete pūrvapakṣa that the siddhānta will refute in the following vimarśas.

**Cross-references:** ĪPK 1.2.1 (nanu svalakṣaṇābhāsaṃ); the Saṃṣi. (apekṣā pāratantryaṃ ca na
saṃbandho jaḍātmanoḥ); Bhartṛhari Vākyapadīya (the relation-verses: nābhidhānaṃ svadharmeṇa); the
yasminsati-maxim (hetūnām anavasthitiḥ). The Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi parallel: the refutation of the
pūrvapakṣa — the self is established as the non-inert self-luminous knower-agent (svatantra
jñātṛ-kartṛ), which the Buddhist's construction (kalpita) cannot explain.

# IPVV Vol 1 — Chunk K: the third vimarśa, the siddhānta's reply, the self-luminous dṛk — T1

*Source: M00020 lines 5750–6300 (continuous). Base: Torella's ĪPK — the third vimarśa (atha tṛtīyo
vimarśaḥ) opens, and the siddhānta replies to the pūrvapakṣa. Covers: the maṅgala-verse of the third
vimarśa (icchāśaktisunirbharam); the reply kārikā 1 (satyaṃ kintu smṛtijñānaṃ pūrvānubhavasaṃskṛteḥ —
memory-cognition does not reveal the prior experience, only rests in the self); kārikā 2 (dṛk svābhāsaiva
nānyena vedyā — perception is self-luminous, not known by another cognition); the jaḍājaḍa (inert/non-inert)
distinction and its four-fold definition; the ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi (v.13); the pramātuḥ (knower) as
self-luminous and not inferable; the Prābhākara and Kaṇāda views refuted; the siddhānta's heart: the 
cognition-continuum needs a non-inert knower (pramātā). Max-effort T1.*

## T1 apparatus — the key decisions (Chunk K)

1. **The third vimarśa opens.** The siddhānta replies to the pūrvapakṣa with the maṅgala-verse
   (icchāśaktisunirbharam — the will-power-full Bhairava). The reply is given by two adhikāras
   (jñāna and kriyā) in the seven verses (ślokasaptaka) beginning "satyaṃ kintu" and ending
   "smṛtyapohanaśaktimān."
2. **The prekṣāpūrvakāra style.** The style of the deliberate user: "not" for the wholly-to-be-
   refuted, "true" for the slightly-to-be-acknowledged, "true but" (satyaṃ kintu) for the 
   slightly-to-be-removed. The Buddhist's refutation of the Sāṅkhya/Kaṇāda cognition is agreed
   (saṃmatam); the 'kintu' asks for the more.
3. **Kārikā 1 (satyaṃ kintu smṛtijñānaṃ).** The memory-cognition, though born from the prior-
   experience impression, rests in the self (ātmaniṣṭhaṃ) — it does not reveal the first experience
   (nādyānubhavavedakam). The experience and the memory are mutually distinct (anyonyabhinnā); the
   memory shines only its own object in its own time (svakāle eva svaviṣayasyaiva), never the
   other's time or object — even in the trikāla-vikalpa ("was/is/will be"), the "this"-ness of the
   object is not actually experienced.
4. **The bāhyavāda refuted.** The external-object view ("the blue shines") makes the manifestation
   enter the object, making the manifestation non-existent (asat) like in the false glass-lump
   cognition. The vyāpaka: the object-embracing form is pervaded by the that-dharma-possessed-ness
   (taddharmāviṣṭatvam); the glass-lump-manifestation lacks it. Hence the know-ness (vedyatva) of
   the external is refuted by the pervader-opposed-pervaded-perception.
5. **The kevala svasaṃvedana.** The sensory/non-sensory division is inner-difference-made by the
   cause and own-form; where no unsādhāraṇa cause is found, the general (autsargika)
   self-perception is used. Even the four-fold-perception-speaker's cognition is self-cognizing.
6. **Kārikā 2 (dṛk svābhāsaiva).** The perception is self-luminous alone, not known by another
   cognition — like the taste-perception is not known by the form-cognition. The experience
   (anubhava), being perception-form, is not known by the memory-cognition. The impression does
   only the object-ness (saviṣayatā) by figurative use; it does not effect the knowledge of the
   prior experience (na tadgatiḥ).
7. **The four-fold rule (caturdhā).** The dṛk svābhāsaiva is explained four ways: (i) own-form-only-
   manifestation (svātmanaḥ prakāśaḥ), (ii) the not-manifesting-has-no-form (svātmā asya prakāśa),
   (iii) never-by-the-other-favor (svātmana eva prakāśate na parasya), (iv) the blue-form is not its
   form (paro'sya na prakāśaḥ). The reverse four-fold defines the inert (jaḍa).
8. **The jaḍājaḍa distinction.** The non-inert (ajaḍa) is that whose own-form is the manifestation
   (prakāśātmā), whose manifestation is rested in itself; the inert (jaḍa) is that which shines
   only by another (its manifestation rests in the knower, not in itself). The blue shines in the
   knower, not in itself — hence it is inert.
9. **The ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi (v.13).** "Thus in the self the asat-like ones are of the manifestation
   alone; the inert ones — the manifestation alone is of the own-self, with the own-other selfs."
   The inert objects are only the manifestation's — the manifestation itself is the non-inert
   knower (ajaḍaḥ pramātā), the great mirror-like unfolding (śaktivijṛmbhā) of Mahādeva.
10. **The pramātā as self-luminous, not inferred.** The knower cannot be inferred as a separate
    thing: the inference only touches the general (sāmānya), never the svalakṣaṇa; hence only the
    apoha/general-form can be the inferred "knower," not the real pramātā. The knower's own
    self-luminousness is not knocked away by the constructed (kalpita) inference — like the cow-ness
    (gotva) is not knocked away by its inference. The parapramātṛ is inferred only as the 
    body-entered manifestation (the other's operation), which actually strengthens the 
    self-luminous-ness.
11. **The Prābhākara and Kaṇāda refuted.** The Prābhākara's "the self is not inert" is reconciled:
    the self shines not as "this" (idam) but in its own way; the aparokṣatā (non-transcendence) is
    the self-luminous-ness (svaprakāśātmatā), not a third manner (which would be the non-being). The
    Kaṇāda's "the cognition is a quality born in the self; the self is inferred by the mind" is
    refuted: the cognition-arising either produces the object's manifest-ness (which is a refuted
    object-dharma) or IS that manifest-ness (the cognition = the manifesting-ness); the object
    cannot be perceptible without its own manifestation.
12. **The svaprakāśa's own inference.** Even though the cognition is non-transcendent with the
    knower, its "being inferred" (by the other's operation) is only the constructed (kalpita) —
    it does not make the supreme-object self-luminous-ness broken. The Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi 20
    (yadyapy arthasthitiḥ) anchors: the object-establishment even in the breath-governed jīva is
    in the supreme self.
13. **The close.** The pramātā is necessarily self-luminous (svaprakāśa) — otherwise there is no
    knower-ness at all (pramātṛtāyā eva ayogāt). The cognition-continuum requires the non-inert
    knower; the Vivṛti's middle passage (the jaḍājaḍa investigation) is the ground for this.

**The crux.** Chunk K is the siddhānta's heart: the reply to the Buddhist pūrvapakṣa. The cognition
is self-luminous (dṛk svābhāsaiva), not known by another cognition; the memory does not reveal the
prior experience but rests in the self. The inert/non-inert distinction grounds the whole: the 
non-inert is the self-luminous manifestation itself, the inert is what shines only in another. The
self-luminous manifestation is the ajaḍa pramātā (the non-inert knower) — the unfolding of Mahādeva's
power. This answers the Buddhist's cognition-continuum: a continuum of non-self-luminous cognitions
cannot explain the knower-ness, the memory, or the object's manifestation.

**Cross-references:** ĪPK 1.2.1/1.2.6/1.2.7 (the pūrvapakṣa-frame), 1.7.3/1.7.14 (deśakālakramajuṣā,
samalo vimalo), 1.3.7 (na cedantaḥ kṛtānantaviśvarūpaḥ), 1.5.16 (svātantryāmukta); the 
Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi 13 and 20; the Yogasūtra; the Prābhākara and Kaṇāda views. The Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi
parallel is the direct anchor for the ajaḍa-pramātṛ (non-inert knower) thesis.

# IPVV Vol 1 — Chunk L: the memory-error (smṛti as bhrānti), the Śaṅkaranandana refutation, the determination — T1

*Source: M00020 lines 6300–6900 (continuous). Base: Torella's ĪPK — the continuation of the siddhānta.
Covers: the paraprakāśyatva of the knower further refuted (the yogi-perception, Yogasūtra 3.20); the
ekapramātṛ (one-knower) and the smṛti-dvaya; kārikā 3 (athātadviṣayatve'pi smṛtestadavasāyataḥ —
memory as error); the Śaṅkaranandana citation on the arthadharmatā of the manifested; kārikā 4
(smṛtitaiva kathaṃ tāvadbhrānteś cārthasthitiḥ katham) — the memory's error, impression, and
object-establishment all refuted; kārikā 5 (bhrāntitve cāvasāyasya na jaḍādviṣayasthitiḥ) — the
determination's error and the object; the two-moon (dvicandra), the timira (eye-defect), the
satkhyāti/asatkhyāti, and the pratibhāsa-as-sattā (appearance as being). The Buddhist's memory-
is-error thesis is fully dissected. Max-effort T1.*

---

## T1 apparatus — the key decisions (Chunk L)

1. **The yogi-perception and the other's cognition.** The other's cognition is known by the yogi-
   perception (Yogasūtra 3.20: pratyayasya paracittajñānaṃ saṃyamāt), not by inference: by the 
   dhyāna-absorption the yogin cultivates non-difference with the other's citta, and (since the 
   bheda-abhimāna is māyā-made) the other-citta shines clearly — it is not inferred. This removes 
   the doubt that the self's manifestation-by-inference is possible.
2. **The ekapramātṛ and the smṛti-dvaya.** "This one experienced" vs "I experienced" — the two
   memories are different-characteristic (vilakṣaṇa). The self-resting (ātmaviśrānta), other-not-
   expecting memory ("I") is the our-meaning (asmadartha); the other-established one is different.
   The manifestation is the self-resting, other-not-expecting (ananyāpekṣā); being known by memory
   is other-expecting — a contradiction.
3. **The anaupādhika characteristic.** The cognition's self-luminous-ness is unconditional 
   (anaupādhikaṃ lakṣaṇam); it does not become otherwise by the object-difference. The otherwise-
   becoming is pervaded by the conditional-ness (aupādhikatva) — which the self-luminous-ness lacks,
   so its otherwise-becoming is negated. Hence the cognition's other-manifested-ness is opposed 
   (viruddham) — jñānasvarūpam anyasaṃvedyaṃ na (the future sūtra).
4. **The atyantaviruddha.** The utterly-opposed is fitted by the reason: the memory-known 
   (smṛtivedya) time — the self-resting I-form (ātmaviśrāntirūpo'ham) would not shine; but the 
   self-luminous/other-manifested are opposed. The dṛk svābhāsaiva is re-established via the 
   svasaṃvedanaikarūpā.
5. **The anyavedyatā via the cause.** The experience is not the memory's object even by cause-ness: 
   if it were, the taste-cognition would be the object of the form-cognition (by the immediately-
   preceding-condition). The distinction is the one-knower-inherent (ekajñātṛsamaveta) cognition-
   ness — the one-object-inherence (ekārthasamavāya) for the Kaṇāda. Without it, Vāsuki's cognition
   would be the object of ours — everyone-all-knower (sarvaḥ sarvajñaḥ), the great turmoil.
6. **The indriya-niyama (sense-organ rule).** The mutual-revealer-ness of the cognitions is rejected:
   the three-fold sense-organ rule (from the organ's force, the organ's fitness, and the number of
   organs) would be lost. The rasa-taste is manifested only with its limitor (upādhi) — the pure 
   taste (kevala) is not manifested by the eye alone (else the ghost-like unseen limitor).
7. **The cakṣurjanitā.** The eye-born cognition does not manifest the taste-cognition (which is 
   non-existent in its own form — like the past experience in memory); it manifests only the 
   error-cognition (sabhramajñāna) with its limitor and the limitor's (the taste). So the reason 
   is not unestablished. The sense-organ-rule-non-being would cause the blind-too-not-blind, etc.
8. **The sākāravāda and the yaugapadya.** In the simultaneous (yaugapadya) mutual-revealer-ness: 
   in the dancer's-seeing, each spectator's cognition would be revealed by the others' — the 
   infinite-dancer's-woman-manifestation (anantanartakyavabhāsa) instead of the one. The lotus-
   mistake (kamalādoṣa) example shows the mixed (vyāmiśra) appearance. So neither order nor 
   simultaneity permits mutual-revealer-ness.
9. **The saṃskāra as niyāmaka refuted.** The impression-born-ness cannot rule (the saṃskāra gives 
   only the similarity, sādṛśyamātra); the graspable/grasper parts of the prior experience are not 
   manifested in the memory. The destroyed (naṣṭa) cannot enter a relation with the memory — the 
   cause-opposed-perception (kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi) of the destroyed-ness.
10. **The ekaviṣayatva (one-object-ness).** Even the Vaiśeṣika (accepting the constant self) cannot 
    establish the memory-experience one-object-ness: there is no third cognition to grasp their 
    similarity — the cause-non-perception (kāraṇānupalabdhi). The figurative use (upacāra) is not 
    the real-vastu-establishment.
11. **Kārikā 3 (memory as error).** The memory does not have the seen-object as a real support; it 
    rests on the object only by error (bhrāntyā dṛṣṭālambanatā). The past father is destroyed — 
    how would he shine? The smārta-father-appearance is place-time-unrestricted and cannot unite 
    with the experiential appearance. The memory is the seen-object by error — this is unfitting 
    (asamañjasam). The Śaṅkaranandana citation (artho na bhāsate bhrāntismṛtyorayogāt) denies the 
    object-dharma-ness of the manifested.
12. **The asad-ātmākhyāti.** The memory supports the not-existing (asad), or (in the ātmākhyāti 
    view) manifests the vāsanā-constructed cognition-ākāra; but never the prior experience or its 
    object — both are non-existent at the memory time. It only determines by the conceit-core 
    (abhimānasāra) — "that was experienced" is the experience-time-touching (anubhavakālasparśa). 
    The three false/self-cognitions (vitathā/asad/ātmākhyāti) are indicated.
13. **Kārikā 4 (smṛtitaiva).** The memory's error-ness, impression-born-ness, and object-establishing- 
    ness are all refuted (sarvatomukham). The memory's primary form (smṛter mukhyaṃ rūpam) — the 
    non-loss (asaṃpramoṣa) of the experienced — is uprooted: the prior experience and its object are 
    wholly hidden (muṣita). The anumāna's error does not establish the object like the memory's 
    (the anumāna has the succession, pāraṃparya; the memory does not). The smṛti is not a vikalpa 
    that is necessarily erroneous.
14. **Kārikā 5 (bhrāntitve cāvasāyasya).** If the determination were erroneous, the object would not 
    be established from the inert (na jaḍād viṣayasthitiḥ); hence in the non-inert, the object-
    establishment rests in the own-rising (nijollekhaniṣṭhānā). The determination (adhyavasāya) is 
    the one that errs (bhramarūpa), not the self-cognition (svasaṃvit) or the non-constructive 
    manifestation.
15. **The dvicandra and the satkhyāti.** The two-moon non-constructive perception is NOT error — the 
    appearance IS the being (pratibhāsa eva sattā); the not-existing cannot shine (asacca khyāti is 
    contradicted). The error is only the determination "this external two-moon is common" 
    (bāhyatāvasāya), which the opposer uproots. The Bhaṭṭa verses (asatyasyābahirbhāvo bādhaḥ 
    sattvam ato dvidhā; ābhāsabhede tv arthaḥ kastatrābhedo bhramo vapuḥ) anchor this. The good 
    Śaṅkaranandana's vijñānaśūnyatā-nīti (bāhyārthaśūnyatā) is justified: the manifestation of the 
    blue is not another's dharma, so its manifestation is self-established (vyāpakānupalabdhi).

**The crux.** Chunk L completes the siddhānta's refutation of the memory-as-error thesis. The 
memory does not reveal the prior experience (only rests in the self — kārikā 1) nor is it error 
(kārikā 3) nor does its determination establish the object by being erroneous (kārikā 5). The 
Śaṅkaranandana's position — that the manifested is not the object's dharma and that the memory 
supports only the not-existing — is refuted by the satkhyāti/pratibhāsa-is-being insight: the 
appearance is the being, so the two-moon non-constructive perception is not error; only the 
external-ness-determination (bāhyatāvasāya) errs. The determination is the error-maker, not the 
self-cognition. This preserves the memory's validity (against the Buddhist's reduction of memory 
to error) and the self-luminous cognition's priority.

**Cross-references:** Yogasūtra 3.20 (paracittajñānaṃ saṃyamāt); ĪPK 1.2.1/1.2.6/1.2.7, 1.3.5 
(bhrāntitve cāvasāyasya); Nyāyasūtra 3.1.19/22/25 (the pūrvajanma-anumāna); Śaṅkaranandana (artho 
na bhāsate); Bhaṭṭa (asatyasyābahirbhāvo bādhaḥ); the satkhyāti/asatkhyāti/ātmākhyāti. The 
Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi parallel: the non-inert self-luminous knower whose appearance is its being.

# IPVV Vol 1 — Chunk M: the jñānādhikāra reflexion core, the anusandhāna, kārikās 6–7 — T1

*Source: M00020 lines 6900–7600 (continuous). Base: Torella's ĪPK — the culmination of the 
jñānādhikāra. Covers: the close of kārikā 5 (the bāhyatāvasāya — external-ness-conclusion as the 
error); kārikā 6 (evam anyonyabhinnānām aparasparavedinām jñānānām anusandhānajanmā naśyen 
janasthitiḥ — the mutual non-knowing cognitions would destroy the tracing-born world-course); the 
anusandhāna (tracing/connecting) as the essence of the knower; kārikā 7 (na ced antaḥkṛtānantaviśvarūpo 
maheśvaraḥ syād ekaścid vapur jñānasmṛtyapohanaśaktimān — unless there be a Maheśvara who has 
interiorized the infinite universe-forms, a single embodiment, powerful in cognition-memory-removal); 
the ekātmatā (one-self-ness) of the cognitions; the vyavahāra (worldly course) requiring it; the 
maheśvara as the one knower. This is the siddhānta's conclusion. Max-effort T1.*

---

## T1 apparatus — the key decisions (Chunk M)

1. **The bāhyatāvasāya as the error.** The error in the magic/eye-defect is only the external-ness-
   conclusion (bāhyatāvasāya) — the appearance itself is the being (pratibhāsa eva sattā). The
   child who sees the shore-trees "running" from the boat is told: it is only the appearance-dharma,
   not a real motion. The non-constructive self-cognition is not error; only the "this external is
   common" determination errs.
2. **The vyavasthā as pramātṛ-dharma, not viṣaya-dharma.** The establishment (vyavasthā) of the
   objects is the knower's dharma (pramātṛdharma), not the object's (viṣayadharma) — because it is
   per-knower-distinct (pratipramātṛ bhidyate), like pleasure. The object-dharma is not per-knower-
   distinct (the white cloth is white for all). Hence the pervader-opposed-pervaded-perception:
   the establishment's being the object-dharma is pervaded by the non-per-knower-distinction.
3. **The saṃvidātmanā.** The determination's operation is the consciousness itself (saṃvid) — not a
   separate thing; the "full manifestation" (pūrṇaḥ prakāśaḥ) is what it is. Where there is no full
   manifestation, there is no error either (like the pleasure's self-cognition) — the 
   vyāpakānupalabdhi. The error is only the memory-determination on the not-object (atīrthe'rthe).
4. **The jaḍājaḍa arrangement (suvyavasthitaḥ).** The inert/non-inert characteristics are well-arranged:
   what is "this"-ness (idantā) — manifested by another, distinct from the manifestation — is inert;
   what is "I"-ness (ahantā) — self-luminous, the manifestation itself — is non-inert. The two are
   mutually opposed and well-divided (pravibhaktaṃ rūpam).
5. **Kārikā 6 (the anusandhāna).** The mutually-distinct, non-mutual-knowing cognitions would destroy
   the tracing-born person-standing (anusandhānajanmā janasthitiḥ). The cognition cannot accept the
   other-cognition's object (unless via the other-cognition-known-ness, which is refuted). The
   desire (arthitā) requires the determination of the object as the pleasure-means — which requires
   the object-mixing (viṣayamelana). Without the tracing, the desire/operation/obtainment/removal-
   taking world-course would perish.
6. **The ekapramātṛ.** The tracing (anusandhāna) is the essence of the knower (pramātā) — the "I"
   cognition (aham idaṃ jānāmi) is I-ness-concluded (ahantāparyavasitam) and prior-later-self-form-
   rehearsal-rested. Without it, the person would be faint-like (mūrcchitaprāyī).
7. **The viṣayamelana refuted for the Buddhist.** The object-mixing cannot be established by the 
   external-object view: the seen-ness (dṛṣṭatā) is not the object's dharma (it is the prior
   cognition-form), nor the cognitions' own-form identity, nor the mutual-revealer-ness. The 
   ālayavijñāna is momentariness-incapable. The sākṣiṇī cognition ("known is this object") is
   refuted via the jñānāntaravedyatā.
8. **The jñānāntaravedyatā (the cognition-known-by-another-cognition) refuted in detail.** The 
   cognition cannot be known by another cognition: the two-manifestation, the pot-example (the
   cognition's manifestation is not the object's dharma), the self-manifestation-necessary-other-
   manifestation (ātmaprakāśananāntarīyaka-paraprakāśana), the aham as the I-manifestation with 
   freedom (ananyamukhaprekṣitva), the Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi 22 (prakāśasyātmaviśrāntirahaṃbhāvaḥ),
   the Naiyāyika's transcendent self refuted, the infinite-regress, and the vyāpakaviruddha.
9. **The lamp-example refuted.** The lamp-lighting-another-lamp analogy fails: the cognition is not 
   the inert (it manifests itself); its manifested-ness (prakāśyatā) does not become its own form
   (like the pot), so it does not become inert. The grāhakasya jñānasya na kācit khaṇḍanā.
10. **The ghaṭasyāpi and the virodha.** Even the pot's being-manifested is not its own dharma; the 
    pervader-opposed-pervaded-perception shows the cognition's own-manifestation (svasaṃvidrūpatva)
    negates its other-cognized-ness (parasaṃvedyatva): the "this"-ness (idantā) is opposed to the 
    "I"-ness (ahantā), which is the consciousness's characteristic. The svabhāva-hetu / 
    viruddhopalabdhi-hetu forms are shown (the śiṃśapā examples).
11. **The naśyet and the ekātmakatā.** If the cognitions were many-selfed (anekātmatā), the world-
    course would necessarily fall (vyāpikā prasajyate). By remainder (pāriśeṣya) the cognitions'
    one inward-face consciousness-tattva form (ekā antarmukha-saṃvittattvasvarūpatā) is established —
    the one self (ekātmatā) of the cognitions.
12. **The bhaṭṭa verses.** vyāpṛttiḥ pratyayasyārthe tatra kiṃcidakurvataḥ — the cognition's operation
    in the object does nothing to it; so the object-dharma-ness of the cognition is not fit, and the
    known-ness of the cognitions is removed. The vyavahāra is pervaded by the one-object-ness 
    (ekaviṣayatvena vyāptaḥ).
13. **Kārikā 7 (na ced antaḥkṛtānantaviśvarūpo maheśvaraḥ).** Unless there is a Maheśvara who has
    interiorized the infinite universe-forms (antaḥkṛtānantaviśvarūpaḥ), a single body 
    (ekaścid vapuḥ), powerful in cognition-memory-removal (jñānasmṛtyapohanaśaktimān) — the 
    establishment fails. The one-self-ness (ekātmatā) of the cognitions is established by the 
    not-deniable practical-activity (vyavahārabalāt).
14. **The śaktayaḥ and the māheśvaryam.** The powers (jñāna/icchā/kriyā, the unmeṣa-nimeṣa) are the
    Lord's supported (tadāśritāḥ), not independent, not separate from his own form — the power-
    joining is his Maheśvar-ness. The consciousness-tattva is the manifestation-form, the wall of all
    cognitions (sakalapramābhittibhūtam), self-established (svayaṃ siddha).
15. **The jaḍa as not-designated-by-the-manifestation.** "The inert shines" is refuted: what is not
    the manifestation's own form cannot be co-referential with it in truth (like the vermilion with
    the blue). The "the inert shines" statement makes the inert the manifestation's form — the
    svabhāva-hetu via the kāraṇānupalabdhi. The Nareśvaraviveka (svayaṃ prāsādo na śveto) anchors.
16. **The bhinnāvabhāsinām.** The distinct-manifesting ones (the objects), though appearing distinct
    by the conceit (abhimāna), are in truth the "I"-manifestation-alone form (ahaṃprakāśamātrasvarūpāḥ)
    — the daṇḍāpūpīya-maxim shows the one knower behind the many manifestations.

**The crux.** Chunk M is the jñānādhikāra's conclusion: the many mutually-non-knowing cognitions 
would destroy the tracing-born world-course (kārikā 6); hence they must share one self (ekātmatā) —
and that one self is the Maheśvara who has interiorized the infinite universe-forms (kārikā 7), the
consciousness-tattva as the manifestation-form wall of all cognitions. The cognition cannot be known
by another cognition (it is self-luminous, its "I"-ness opposed to the "this"-ness of the inert);
the establishment of the objects is the knower's dharma; and the distinct appearances are in truth
the one self-luminous manifestation. This is the siddhānta's positive culmination, answering the 
Buddhist pūrvapakṣa completely.

**Cross-references:** ĪPK 1.2.1/1.2.6/1.2.7, 1.3.2 (dṛk svābhāsaiva), 1.3.5 (bhrāntitve cāvasāyasya),
1.5.3 (prakāśātmā prakāśyo'rthaḥ), 1.5.14 (sā sphurattā), 1.5.16 (svātantryāmukta); the 
Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi 22 (prakāśasyātmaviśrāntirahaṃbhāvaḥ); the Nareśvaraviveka (svayaṃ prāsādo na 
śveto; nīlādikoparāgeṇa; pareṣām api keśādau); the Bhaṭṭa (vyāpṛttiḥ pratyayasyārthe); the 
āgama-verses (tathatāvyutthito buddhaḥ, puṃsāmanugrahārthāya, yathā prakṣyanti te śiṣyāḥ). The 
Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi parallel is the direct anchor: the ajaḍa-pramātṛ (non-inert knower) as the 
self-luminous one whose manifestation is the objects.

# IPVV Vol 1 — Chunk N: the close — the maheśvara's śaktis, the apoha, the colophon — T1

*Source: M00020 lines 7600–8313 (continuous, the end of the file). Base: Torella's ĪPK — the
culmination of kārikā 7 (na ced antaḥkṛtānantaviśvarūpo maheśvaraḥ) and the close of the
jñānādhikāra / third vimarśa. Covers: the tādrūpya (that-form-ness) of the cognitions with the 
I-part; the aham aṃśa; the sādharmya-vaidharmya; the jñāna as self-luminous one-form; the 
non-perception (anupalabdhi) of the absence; the Dharmakīrti verses (ekopalambhānubhavāt); the 
smṛti/vikalpa and the sparśajñāna; kārikā 7's śaktis (jñāna/smṛti/apohana); the viśvarūpatā and 
the māyā-pramātṛ; the śakti as the bhāva's own form; the Gītā citations (11.7/8/26); the apoha 
(vikalpa) as the apohanaśakti; and the colophon. This is the volume's final argument and its close. 
Max-effort T1.*

## T1 apparatus — the key decisions (Chunk N)

1. **The tādrūpya (that-form-ness).** The cognitions, manifesting with the I-part excess
   (ahamaṃśātirekeṇa), have the supreme-real manifestation-self-I-ness-that-form-ness
   (prakāśātmakāhantātādrūpyam) unbroken even in the māyā-state. The excess/non-pervasion/
   non-eternality are the object-facing-limitor-made (viṣayaunmukhyopādhikṛta); the māyā (the
   Lord's power) does not cover the own-form (śaktyā śaktimatāmanāvaraṇāt).
2. **The ekavākya of naśyet / na cet.** The vṛttikṛt joins "would-perish the person-standing"
   (naśyet janasthitiḥ) and "not-if the Maheśvara" (na cet) into one statement via the 
   hetumallīṅā. The tracing (anusandhāna) of all the objects' cognitions is the consciousness-
   tattva itself (aśeṣapadārthajñānānāmanyonyānusandhānaṃ cittattvam) — the one inward-face
   consciousness, not a separate thing.
3. **The kevala-pradeśa (the alone-place).** The alone-place cognition (kevalapradeśajñānaṃ, the 
   "no pot here" place) is the key test: the pot's absence is not established by the separate 
   non-perception (which would need an infinite regress), but by the pervader-opposed-pervaded-
   perception. The aghaṭa is a paryudāsa (the other-vastu manifestation), not a prasajyapratiṣedha.
4. **The Dharmakīrti verses.** ekopalambhānubhavād idaṃ nopalabhe iti... — the non-perception is 
   established by perception alone; otherwise the non-being-ness of the object would be known from 
   the non-perception and the non-being-ness of the perception by another — the infinite regress. 
   The anupalabdhi of the absent second cognition is not a separate pramāṇa.
5. **The rūpa-sparśa and the vikalpa/smṛti.** The touch-cognition and the form-cognition (different 
   sense-organs) cannot be co-cognized: the vikalpa cannot refute the prior form-cognition (it is 
   not the not-that-form vikalpa); the memory only imitates the prior experience, it does not 
   manifest it as object (jñānānāṃ parasaṃvedyatvasya nirākṛtatvāt). The smṛti's anukaraṇa means it 
   cannot reveal the co-being (sahabhāva) of the two cognitions.
6. **The ekasvasaṃvedana-viśrānta.** When there is one inward-face consciousness-tattva (not 
   separate self-cognitions), the two cognitions, if simultaneous, would rest in the one self-
   cognition and manifest as one — which does not happen (the darkness-time "I do not see the 
   form"). Hence the one self-cognition is established (svātmani rūpajñānaṃ nāstīti niścinvan).
7. **The ananyāpekṣa and the ekam antarmukham.** "Who are you whose pot-cognition?" — the other-
   cognition-known-ness leads to the infinite regress and the loss of the own-other division. Hence 
   the other-not-expecting self-luminous "I" (ananyāpekṣaprakāśam aham) is the one inward-face 
   consciousness-tattva, which removes all the confusions (samastaviplavāvakāśābhāvaḥ).
8. **The smṛtyādi and the svācchandya.** The many cognitions are traced by the one inward-face 
   (which manifests as-much-as it wills — svecchāvaśāt yāvaj jighṛkṣati tāvat pratyavabhāsate), so 
   there is no simultaneity-all-tracing-fall. The niḥstimita (non-flashing) would be the inert-ness; 
   the vimarśa (reflexive-awareness) is the Bhagavat's power-particular (sphurattāspandādi).
9. **The jñāna-smṛti-apohana śaktis.** The Bhagavat's powers are jñāna (manifestation), smṛti 
   (the inward-face form's rehearsal of the prior outward-face — the memory that enables the 
   vyavahāra of the momentary appearances), and apohana (the vikalpa's removal of the suspected 
   opponents). The phalabheda (result-difference) is why the one power is spoken of in the plural — 
   the fire is burner/cooker/illuminator; the one power is the bhāva's own form, not separate 
   (the Mālinīvijayavārttika 3.5, Mālinītantra 4.5 verses).
10. **The viśvarūpatā and the māyā-pramātṛ.** The Bhagavat, from his freedom, separates a being from 
    the manifestation and manifests it; the māyā-pramātṛ is the contracted manifestation. The 
    māyā-pramātṛ's outward-face form is the new-new cognition; the aiśvara svātantrya is the 
    jñānaśakti. The Gītā 11 (the viśvarūpa-darśana) is cited: Arjuna sees the universe in the 
    body — the paramātman's own. The anyonyātmatā (mutual-self-ness) of the beings is the 
    īśvarāṅgatā (the Lord's limb-ness).
11. **The apoha and the svalakṣaṇa.** The vikalpa is the apohanaśakti: it removes the suspected 
    not-that-doers (like the pot suspected of the many-opponents by the object-action). The 
    anyonyātmatā makes the "not-that-form" (atadrūpatā) possible. The ācāryapāda verses 
    (yāvatyo'rthakriyāstāvatsaṃkhyo'tatkāriṇāṃ gaṇaḥ; ekapratyavamarśo yastatkāriṣu bahuṣvapi) 
    anchor this. The svalakṣaṇa's being-manifested has no opposite to be suspected (the 
    Bhaṭṭa's apoha is refuted; the niḥsvabhāvatva would make the blue/yellow vikalpas identical).
12. **The māyīyatā and the paramārtha.** The māyā-position (the pramātṛ-prameya bheda) is the 
    not-rehearsed (avimṛśyamāna) one-form-entry of all in the manifestation — the real is the 
    tādātmya (identity), the ekarūpāveśa (one-form-entry). The māyā does not remove it (else no 
    manifestation); it only withholds the rehearsal (the neti-parāmarśa). This is the 
    viśvātmatva (universe-self-ness) that is not unmanifested.
13. **The Bhagavat's vikalpavyāpāra.** The Bhagavat himself does not have the new-manifestation/
    memory/construction dharmas (they arise in the māyā-pramātṛs from his freedom); his freedom 
    IS the jñānādi-śaktis. But in the Īśvara-state he accepts the "not" (neti) rehearsal — the 
    apohanaśakti is present even there (the "idam aham" co-reference needs it). The contraction 
    (saṃkoca) of the sarvajñatā means his māyā-ness is not for him.
14. **The mattaḥ and the fifth-case.** The Gītā's "from me" (mattaḥ) — the cause-ness/support-ness 
    of the own-self — is the pañcamī; the lyab-elision in hetau (matsāmarthyādetat). The 
    jñāna/smṛti/apohana are the same cognition-power variously used; the two new powers are not 
    separate from the jñānaśakti (tānyeva ca śaktir iti).
15. **The colophon.** The third vimarśa (paradarśanānupapattivimarśaḥ) in the jñānādhikāra closes 
    — and with it Vol 1 of the Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī.

**The crux.** Chunk N completes the volume: the maheśvara of kārikā 7 is the one consciousness-
tattva whose manifestation-freedom is the cognitions' tracing, memory, and removal (the apoha); the 
universe-forms are interiorized in him (antaḥkṛtānantaviśvarūpaḥ); the māyā-pramātṛs are the 
contracted manifestations of the one freedom; and the paramārtha is the one-form-entry (ekarūpāveśa) 
of all in the manifestation, with the bheda being only the withheld rehearsal. The self-luminous 
cognition, the ajaḍa-pramātṛ, and the maheśvara are one — this is the siddhānta's final, complete 
statement, closing the third vimarśa and the volume.

**Cross-references:** ĪPK 1.2.1/1.2.6/1.2.7, 1.3.2 (dṛk svābhāsaiva), 1.3.5 (bhrāntitve cāvasāyasya), 
1.5.3 (prakāśātmā prakāśyo'rthaḥ), 1.5.14 (sā sphurattā), 1.6.3 (tadatatpratibhābhājā), 1.6.11 
(ata eva yathābhīṣṭaḥ), 2.2.1 (kriyāsaṃbandhasāmānya); the Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi 20/22; the 
Nareśvaraviveka; the Dharmakīrti verses (ekopalambhānubhavāt); the Vijñānabhairava 19–20; the 
Mālinīvijayavārttika 3.5; the Mālinītantra 4.5; the Bhaṭṭa (vyāpṛttiḥ pratyayasyārthe; 
nacābhāvo viśiṣyate); the ācāryapāda apoha-verses; the Bhagavadgītā 11.7/8/26; the ācārya-
mūrti verse (ācāryamūrtimāsthāya). The Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi parallel is the direct anchor.

# IPVV Vol 2 — Chunk V2-A: the caturtho vimarśa — the smṛti, the ahaṃ, the kāla-śakti — T1

*Source: M00021 lines 29–700 (continuous). Base: Torella's ĪPK — the fourth vimarśa (atha caturtho
vimarśaḥ). Covers: the opening maṅgala (īśvaram aśeṣatāpaprāśamanam); the connection of the smṛti to
the siddhānta (the kārikā 1: sa hi pūrvānubhūtārthopalabdhā, parato'pi san, vimṛśan sa iti svairī
smaratīty apadiśyate); the kāla (time) and the kāla-śakti; the svairitva (freedom); the smaraṇa as
the paramaṃ svātantryam; the vimarśa (reflexive-awareness) and its two times; the māyā-pramātṛ; the
anubhava/asaṃpramoṣa; the kārikā 2 (bhāsayecca svakāle'rthātpūrvābhāsitam āmṛśan); the svalakṣaṇa;
the parāmarśa as the prakāśa's own nature; the liṅ (vidhi) analysis. The smṛti is established as the
Lord's own power (smṛtiśakti) — the paramaṃ svātantryam. Max-effort T1.*

## T1 apparatus — the key decisions (Chunk V2-A)

1. **The smṛti as the Lord's power.** The fourth vimarśa opens by establishing the memory (smṛti) as
   the Lord's own power (smṛtiśakti) — the paramaṃ svātantryam (supreme freedom). The order (jñāna →
   smṛti → apohana) is stated, but the smṛti is taken first because it was the one "not-if" (na cet)
   established in the previous siddhānta (Vol 1) — the prasaṅga-reversal gives the self-Lord's
   establishment, and the smṛti is that atiśayam abhijñānam.
2. **Kārikā 1 (sa hi pūrvānubhūtārthopalabdhā).** The free-one (svairī) Maheśvara, being the perceiver
   of the prior-experienced object even in the other time, reflecting "that" (sa iti), remembers. The
   key: the prior-later both-times are the vimarśa's two times; the vimarśa's freedom (svairitva) is
   the paramaṃ svātantryam. The Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi, the Divākara citations, and the dhyānādibhāvaṃ
   smṛtireva verse anchor this.
3. **The kāla (time) and the kāla-śakti.** The avabhāsana (manifestation) is the creation-action; the
   kartṛśakti is the avabhāsanā. The time-order (krama) is the co-being-non-being (asahabhāva) of the
   manifestations, raised by the kālaśakti (the kālotthāpakatva). The bhūtādi-kāla-mixed
   avabhāsanā is the kriyā. The potter's making (kumbhakaraṇa) is the same — the param-Lord's cognition
   not other than the potter's cognition (2.4.21: itthaṃ tathā... icchaiva hetutā kartṛtā kriyā).
4. **The smṛtikriyā and the tamas.** In the māyā-pramātṛ, the memory is the inward-face (antarmukha)
   form's rehearsal of the prior outward-face; the remembered object is covered (tamasā avacchādita),
   and the vimarśa's clarification (sphuṭīkaraṇa) is the icchā's beginning (upakrama) — the susmūrṣā.
   The Spandakārikā 16 (natu yo'ntarmukho bhāvaḥ) and 33 (yathā icchābhyarthitaḥ) are cited.
5. **The smartṛtva of the body refuted.** The body/breath-eight's rememberer-ness is only the
   superimposed-freedom (samāropitasvātantrya); the consciousness-part is not divided from the
   Bhagavat (cidaṃśastu na bhagavato bhidyate). The jñānamāla (the Buddhist's cognition-series)
   cannot establish the memory (kāryakāraṇabhāvena bheda is refuted via dṛk svābhāsaiva 1.3.2).
6. **The māyā-pramātṛ's memory.** The māyā-knower cannot remember the fainted or the unseen without
   the rule (aniyatatva); the unseen's ruler is the consciousness-tattva-form Lord (the 
   īśvaraprerito verse from the Gītā). The param-self enters the turya/suṣupta seed-ground
   (bījabhū), then manifests the dream-ground — the "it remembers" is that manifestation.
7. **The ekatva, vibhutva, kartṛtva.** The freedom/oneness/agent-ness of the māyā-knower are ended in
   the param-Lord's form (parameśvararūpaparyavasitāni). The vibhutva is vividhaṃ kṛtvā bhavati — not
   the mere vyāpakatva (the kāla and deśa are vedyabhūmipraviṣṭa; the Divākaravatsa verse dūrānti-
   deśādigatārkacandra...). The viṣaya-bheda objection to the memory is removed.
8. **The asaṃpramoṣa-smaraṇa.** The memory is the experience's non-loss (asaṃpramoṣa) — the not-utter-
   loss of the prior manifestation; but it is not the experience itself (the ghaṭa/gau example: the
   cow is a different object). The kevalam: the ekībhāva with the blue-manifestation-part (the common
   object) across the other knowers (sarvajñakrimiprabhṛti) is what the māyā-pramātṛ enters by the 
   tādātmya-union (sāyujya) — the "ahaṃ nīlaṃ bhāsayāmi" (1.6.7). This is the creation (nirmāṇa), not
   the prior-being memory.
9. **The apohana (removal) and the niścaya.** The determination (niścaya) is apohana-form — it removes
   the not-that-form (atadrūpa) superimpositions. The kālabheda is not real (avāstava), so the
   "I-experience-now" (idam aham idānīmeva anubhavāmīti) conceit is the memory-identity (tādātmya).
   The Śaṅkaranandana/Dharmottara verses (siddhaṃ siddhatayā vastu nirūpyaṃ na tathā tataḥ) are cited.
10. **The pratyabhijñāna and the tulyakālatā.** When the two (the object and the experience) are united,
    the recognition (so'yam iti) arises. The one-rehearsal/one-prescription gives the two differences;
    the equal-rehearsal/prescription gives the two. The yogin superimposes the prior time on the
    object, not on the experience.
11. **Kārikā 2 (bhāsayecca svakāle'rthātpūrvābhāsitam āmṛśan).** The memory's object is the svalakṣaṇa
    (with the prior place-time avaccheda, the deśa-kāla-saṃkoca-core); the parāmarśa necessarily
    involves the manifestation (prakāśanāntarīyaka); the parāmarśa is the prakāśa's own nature
    (svabhāva) — the svabhāva-hetu: "of the object, the rehearsal is manifestation-self, from its
    own-nature-ness." The nirviṣayatva of the vikalpas is refuted (they are viṣayavat via the
    sāmānyalakṣaṇa); the memory's ekaviṣayatva establishes the one cognition-tattva.
12. **The liṅ (vidhi) analysis.** The long digression on the ākhyāta/liṅ: the action is the primary
    expressed (kriyaiva mukhyam abhidheyam); the vidhi is the niyoga (rule); the "juhuyāt svargakāmaḥ"
    is "he-sacrifices-alone" (juhoty eva); the liṅ's kālaviśeṣa is not expressed but the nitya-
    pravṛtta-vartamāna is shown. This is a grammatical interlude connecting to the kriyādhikāra.
13. **The present-rehearsal.** The vārtamānika-vimarśa, being, does not give the vastu's that-time-ness
    but only rests in the non-removal of the prior manifestation-rehearsal. The pūrvaprakāśitavimṛṣṭa
    is the asaṃpramoṣa; the pūrvaprakāśitatva is why the manifestation is avaccheda-ed by the place
    etc. (the yesterday-water/friend/pot example).

**The crux.** Chunk V2-A establishes the smṛti as the Lord's own power (smṛtiśakti = paramaṃ 
svātantryam): the free-one (svairī) Maheśvara, who has the aśeṣakālānugata (all-time-following) 
awareness, reflects "that" (sa iti) and remembers. The memory's two times are the vimarśa's; the
manifestation (avabhāsana) is the creation-action, and the time-order is the kālaśakti's raising.
The māyā-pramātṛ's memory is the contracted manifestation of the one freedom; the svalakṣaṇa's
rehearsal necessarily manifests, since the parāmarśa is the prakāśa's own nature. This is the 
fourth vimarśa's opening argument, continuing the siddhānta's positive account of the Lord's powers.

**Cross-references:** ĪPK 1.2.3/1.3.1/1.3.2 (dṛk svābhāsaiva), 1.6.7 (tadevaṃ vyavahāre'pi prabhur
dehādim āviśan), 2.1.4 (kramo bhedāśrayo), 2.3.4 (dīrghavṛttordhva), 2.4.21 (itthaṃ tathā ghaṭapaṭādy);
the Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi; the Spandakārikā 16/33; the Bodhapramātṛsiddhi 8 (paricchinnaprakāśatvaṃ);
the Divākara verses (sarve'nubhūtā yadi; saṃpreṣite cetasi; dūrāntideśādigatārkacandra); the
Bhaṭṭa-Śaṅkaranandana (siddhaṃ siddhatayā vastu); the Gītā (ajño jantur anīśo'yam); the Vyākaraṇa
(Patañjali, the liṅ/niyoga analysis). The Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi parallel is the direct anchor for the
ajaḍa-pramātṛ's freedom.
